title: Key Projection — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Key Vector Generation and Attention Matching · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Seven user-supplied questions, length-balanced choices, unique teaching diagrams, and short explanations with optional detail.
hero:
KEY PROJECTION · VISUAL MODULE MAP

Query asks; Key describes; attention scores the match.

Keys are learned numerical vectors. The matching scores become attention weights that determine how Values are blended; scores here are illustrative.

questions.stem: What is Key Projection in Transformer models, and how does it create Key vectors that help other tokens determine whether the information represented by a particular token is relevant to them?
options: Key vectors are fixed word labels attached during tokenization, so a Transformer does not need learned matrices to compare different token features.
Key projection uses a learned matrix to make matching features from each token, allowing other tokens' Queries to estimate how relevant it is.
Key projection chooses the final output word directly, without producing any score against Query vectors or using information from other positions.
Key vectors copy already generated words after attention is complete, rather than representing available input features during the attention calculation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a public library where every book has searchable tags. A Key vector is similar to those tags: it describes features a token can offer to other tokens. The Transformer creates that Key using a learned weight matrix applied to the token's representation. Another token's Query can compare against it to judge relevance. Keys do not contain final answers or fixed dictionary labels. They provide a learned way to find which positions may contain useful context.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: A Transformer learns separate linear projections for Queries, Keys, and Values. For a token representation x, a Key is k=xW_K, where W_K is learned during training. It is not a fixed tag or dictionary entry. Queries from different token positions score each Key via a dot product, so Keys provide a learned matching interface. Attention scores become normalized weights that combine Values, not Keys.
questions.figure:
01 · What Key Projection does

Each token becomes a Key vector through the same learned projection

The diagram depicts learned features, not literal numerical values. Each input position gets its own projected Key.

questions.stem: How does a Key vector differ from a Query vector in Self-Attention, and why can we think of a Query as something searching for information and a Key as something describing what information is available?
options: Queries hold content to return to the output, while Keys represent the final generated answer. Matching happens before any final words are chosen.
Query and Key vectors are identical copies of each token's original embedding, so their separate names cannot change how attention matches information.
Keys ask which token to look for, while Queries describe what every candidate offers; this reverses their usual matching responsibilities.
Queries represent what a token seeks, while Keys describe features offered by candidate tokens, so matching scores can connect useful information.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Suppose a detective searches a case file for evidence about a missing phone. The detective's request resembles a Query; labels on file entries resemble Keys. A matching entry may contain details, represented by its Value. Inside self-attention, separate learned matrices create these vectors from token features. The Query asks what would help, the Key supports matching, and the Value carries information into the result. Different projections let the model learn these three roles separately.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: For the same input token representation xᵢ, Query qᵢ=xᵢW_Q and Key kᵢ=xᵢW_K use separate learned weight matrices. A Query is a useful analogy for what a token is looking for; a Key is the candidate's matching descriptor. Their dot product scores relevance. The Value vⱼ=xⱼW_V is what gets passed to the attention output after weights are applied. These are learned numeric roles, not manually labeled semantic categories.
questions.figure:
02 · Query versus Key

Query and Key match; the corresponding Value supplies information

A token can produce all three projections. Their roles differ because each uses separately learned weights.

questions.stem: When a Transformer processes the sentence "The animal was hungry because it had not eaten," how does Key Projection help the token "it" attend to relevant tokens such as "animal" through Query-Key matching?
options: The Query for “it” can match the Key for “animal,” helping attention recognize that the earlier noun provides useful context for the pronoun.
The Key for “it” directly replaces the word “animal” before any Query-Key scores are calculated, so no relevance comparison is required.
The earlier word “animal” becomes a Value only after its Key turns into a Query, because the different projections are applied one after another.
The Query for “animal” always selects “it,” because pronouns receive fixed highest scores regardless of sentence meaning or learned matching features.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Read “The animal was hungry because it had not eaten.” To understand “it,” the model compares that token's Query with Keys from “animal,” “hungry,” and the other words. A strong match with “animal” can help the representation capture the intended reference. Key projection does not replace one word with another. It supplies numerical features for relevance scoring. These weights are learned from data, so matching depends on context rather than a fixed pronoun rule.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: In the sentence “The animal was hungry because it had not eaten,” the token “it” forms a Query from its current representation. “Animal” has a Key derived from its representation. If they match relatively strongly, the model can assign weight to the earlier token and use its Value information. Other tokens may also receive weight. Not every attention head resolves coreference, and an individual attention score is not by itself a faithful explanation of the model's reasoning.
questions.figure:
03 · Matching in context

The Query for “it” may strongly match the Key for “animal”

The curved path is an illustration of possible attention behavior, not a deterministic pronoun-resolution rule.

questions.stem: How does Key Projection mathematically transform hidden-state vectors using the equation \(K = XW_K\), and how do the learned weight matrix, tensor dimensions, and scaled dot product \(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k}\) contribute to attention score calculation?
options: Key projection multiplies Softmax probabilities by learned weights after attention has finished, rather than creating token features used in matching scores.
Key projection merges every token into one shared vector before calculating attention, so different positions and heads cannot offer separate matching information.
Key projection maps hidden states through learned weights; Query-Key dot products scaled by head dimension then produce scores used to calculate attention.
Key projection divides inputs by the sequence length and calculates attention without any Query vectors, learned Key weights, or token-level matching operations.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a system examining a short weather bulletin. Let its hidden states be X[T,8], with T token positions and eight features each. Multiply by learned Key weights WK[8,4] to obtain K[T,4]. Queries with compatible feature width compare against the transposed Key matrix. Dividing the dot products by √dₖ controls their scale before Softmax. The result is a score table describing potential attention links, not a list of final words.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Without batch dimension, let X have shape [T,d_model] and W_K have shape [d_model,H_k·d_k]. The Key matrix K_flat=XW_K has shape [T,H_k·d_k] and reshapes to [H_k,T,d_k]. Independently projected Query heads have compatible per-head dimension d_k. With equal numbers of Q and K heads, each attention head computes score matrix S=QKᵀ/√d_k, of shape [T,T]. The division by √d_k stabilizes dot-product magnitude before masking and Softmax. For grouped/multi-query attention, H_q can exceed H_k, so Key/Value heads must be shared or mapped across Query groups rather than multiplied head-by-head without alignment.
questions.figure:
04 · Mathematics and tensor dimensions

Multiplying X by W_K creates Keys used in scaled dot-product scores

Illustrative shapes: T=3, d_model=4, Hk=2 and dk=2. Head-sharing variants align Query heads differently.

questions.stem: How can Key Projection be implemented using Python and PyTorch, including defining a learnable Key projection matrix, transforming input token representations, organizing Keys into multiple attention heads, and comparing them with Query vectors to calculate attention scores?
options: PyTorch creates one constant Key vector for all token positions and repeats it across every head, preventing context-dependent matching representations.
Use a PyTorch linear layer to create learned Keys, reshape them into attention heads, and multiply Queries by transposed Keys to calculate matching scores.
Use raw token identifiers as Keys and add them to Queries without converting them into compatible learned vectors or organizing the heads.
Create Keys by applying Softmax directly to token IDs, then train the projection without gradients so the matching matrix remains unchanged.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Picture a small PyTorch model reading descriptions of museum exhibits. A learnable nn.Linear layer turns each input representation into a Key vector. Reshape those Keys so they are organized by attention head. Project Queries separately, then compute Q @ K.transpose(-2,-1) to obtain matching scores for each head. Check the output shapes and apply scaling before Softmax. This shows why Key vectors must have compatible feature dimensions with Queries, rather than being raw vocabulary IDs.
questions.technicalExplanation:
Detailed explanation: The code below creates learnable Query and Key projections, shapes their outputs into two heads, then calculates scaled dot-product attention scores. Its tensor shapes and Softmax row totals were checked with PyTorch on CPU.
import math
import torch
from torch import nn

torch.manual_seed(2)
B, T, d_model, heads, dk = 1, 4, 8, 2, 4
x = torch.randn(B, T, d_model)
to_key = nn.Linear(d_model, heads * dk, bias=False)
to_query = nn.Linear(d_model, heads * dk, bias=False)

def split_heads(t):
    return t.reshape(B, T, heads, dk).transpose(1, 2)

K = split_heads(to_key(x))
Q = split_heads(to_query(x))
scores = Q @ K.transpose(-2, -1) / math.sqrt(dk)
weights = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
print("K:", tuple(K.shape))           # (1, 2, 4, 4)
print("scores:", tuple(scores.shape)) # (1, 2, 4, 4)
print(weights.sum(-1))               # each row sums to 1
In decoder-only Transformers, a causal mask should prevent attention to future tokens before Softmax. MQA/GQA additionally requires explicit sharing or mapping of Key heads to Query heads.

questions.stem: How are Key vectors modified by Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), and why does applying compatible positional rotations to Queries and Keys allow Attention scores to capture relative token positions while preserving positional information?
options: Rotate Query and Key coordinate pairs consistently by position so their matching scores can represent relative distance between tokens while retaining learned content.
Rotate only the Keys but leave Queries unchanged, which guarantees every attention score depends solely on relative distance instead of token content.
Apply the RoPE rotation to Values after Softmax, leaving Query-Key scores unchanged and expecting positional information to appear in matching anyway.
Add absolute position numbers to the lengths of Key vectors, making Query-Key dot products independent of the relative position between tokens.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Suppose the words “launch” and “rocket” appear several positions apart in a technical announcement. RoPE rotates the Query and Key coordinate pairs according to their locations. Comparing the rotated vectors can then reflect the words' relative distance, along with their learned content relationships. Both Query and Key rotations are needed for this usual property. Rotating only the Value vector after Softmax would not add the same positional information to Query-Key matching.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: RoPE rotates pairs of coordinates within each projected Query and Key vector. At positions m and n, Q and K use compatible angle frequencies based on those positions. Because R(mθ)ᵀR(nθ)=R((n−m)θ), the resulting dot product can represent the relative position difference. The vectors still depend on token content. Implementations may use different frequency scales or context-extension adjustments. RoPE is usually applied to Query and Key components, not Value components.
questions.figure:
06 · Rotary Position Embeddings

Compatible position-based rotations let Query–Key scores reflect token distance

RoPE encodes relative displacement through paired rotations. It does not make all attention scores depend only on distance.

questions.stem: How does Key Projection affect memory consumption and inference speed in autoregressive Large Language Models, and how do KV caching, Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), and compressed Key representations reduce computational and memory overhead while maintaining attention quality?
options: KV caching stores only final output logits, while MQA and GQA reduce the size of the vocabulary rather than changing Key-Value head organization.
KV caching removes every attention computation after the first token, and MQA no longer needs Values because the Keys hold complete final answers.
MQA maintains independent Key heads for every Query, while GQA stores separate Key copies for each head, reversing their intended sharing efficiencies.
KV caching reuses earlier Keys and Values; MQA shares one KV head and GQA shares groups, reducing memory used during autoregressive generation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine a chatbot writing a long itinerary one token at a time. Recomputing the Keys and Values of every earlier token wastes work. A KV cache stores representations that generation can reuse. In ordinary MHA, Query heads generally have separate KV heads. MQA shares one KV head, while GQA uses several shared groups. Sharing can reduce cache memory and bandwidth. Attention still needs to compare new Queries with earlier Keys, so caching does not eliminate all computation.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: KV caching stores previous token Keys and Values during autoregressive inference so they do not have to be reprojected at every generated token. The new Query still scores the growing KV cache, and memory grows with sequence length. A rough KV cache budget is 2·batch·layers·context_length·kv_heads·head_dim·bytes_per_element, ignoring padding/metadata. Standard multi-head attention can use one KV head per Query head. Multi-Query Attention (MQA) uses one shared KV head; Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares a smaller number of KV heads across Query groups. Compressed or low-rank Keys can save more memory but may add reconstruction cost or affect quality. Savings in KV storage and bandwidth do not eliminate attention computation.
questions.figure:
07 · KV caching, MQA and GQA

Caching reuses past Keys; shared KV heads reduce memory and bandwidth

A smaller KV cache saves bandwidth, but attention to the growing context still has computational cost. Quality can change with KV sharing.
